title: Secatogue Ancestral Land
summary: Secatogue homelands are remembered along Great South Bay, east of Massapequa, across tidal creeks, neck lands, inland routes, and south shore villages. Records connect the name with Secatogue country and with neighboring Massapequa, Merrick, Setauket, and central Long Island Native histories.
why_this_matters: Secatogue Ancestral Land presents Great South Bay creeks, marshes, and inland routes as Native geography. It also connects older records to descendant community memory and the continued presence of Native families on Long Island.
introduction_title: Secatogue People And Great South Bay
introduction_content: Secatogue is one of the names repeated in the old "thirteen tribes" list, but historian John A. Strong's critique of that framework cautions against reading the list as a complete pre-contact political map. The name is best understood as a place-based record of people living in relation to bay, creek, meadow, and inland routes, not as a complete description of government. The people behind the name were not confined to the neat borders that deeds and later maps tried to impose. Their histories continued through kinship, movement, land records, descendant memory, and relationships with neighboring communities.
history_content: The name Sichetanyhacky appears in Dutch-period records as a land or country name for the Secatogue people. It is tied to the eastern boundary of Massapeag jurisdiction and to Secatogue territory on the south shore.
translation_content: Sichetanyhacky is interpreted as the country or land of the Secatogues. Recorded forms include Siketenwhacky, Siketenhacky, and Sickentanhacky.
preservation_content: Some Secatogue histories involve camps, village sites, family places, and archaeological traces. The public story stays at the level of the broader south shore landscape.
land_loss_content: Secatogue history is tied to south shore tidal creeks, bay travel, colonial deed records, community gatherings, and later descendant history. Land records and colonial restrictions show Native presence under increasing pressure rather than disappearance.
geometry_cleanup_notes: The Babylon/Islip south-shore mainland, Great South Bay-facing necks and marsh islands, Captree/Robert Moses land, and western Fire Island. This corrects the former mainland-only display but does not claim a precise territorial line through Great South Bay or Fire Island.
